ca_shute_mills_area.blurb: The Shute-Mills Area is the main cluster of small formations on the far side of Mount St. Helena, a short hike beyond the Bubble. The rocks are only around fifty feet tall, with pocketed, moderately steep faces and a mix of bolted lines and trad cracks. Many cracks and horizontal slots take good gear, so bring a rack if you want the full range. Most grades fall between 5.8 and 5.10, with a few easier and a handful harder. Mystery Hole and The Chief are among the standouts. Traffic is light, and poison oak grows beside the trail, so long pants help.

ca_saddle_rocks_skirt_west_face.blurb: The Skirt is the broad west-facing wall of Saddle Rocks, a large formation that stands out across this part of Joshua Tree. It is almost entirely trad, with crack and slab lines that run from mellow to difficult, and the bulk of the grades sit in the 5.9 to 5.11 range. Walk on the Wild Side is the easy way up the face, while Where Have all the Cowboys Gone and Harlequin are the harder classics. Expect little shade and a wide-open feel, so the cooler months are the comfortable ones.
ca_saddle_rocks_skirt_west_face.parking_note: Use the big paved lot on Park Boulevard at the Hall of Horrors. A marked path leaves from it and heads east to the base of the face.

ca_g_church_bowl.blurb: Church Bowl is a roadside granite crag on the north side of Yosemite Valley, between the village and the Ahwahnee. It is one of the Valley's easiest places to reach for moderate climbing, mostly trad cracks with some sport lines and a little aid. Bishops Terrace is the best-known line, a classic 5.8 hand crack, and harder sport routes such as Energizer and 700 Club sit nearby. Because it is so close to the road it can get crowded, and the sloping ledges are slick when damp.
ca_g_church_bowl.approach: A short walk in from the road on the Valley's north side; a trail follows the base of the wall past the main routes.

ca_first_corridor_the.blurb: The First Corridor is a narrow, steep-sided gully in Texas Canyon, in the Angeles National Forest above the Los Angeles basin. The climbing is bolted face and slab on conglomerate, with most routes between 5.8 and 5.11, including Welcome to Texas Canyon, Holy Mole and Power Fingers. Holds on this stone can snap off, and it stays damp for days after a storm, so it is best climbed only when the ground at the base is completely dry.

ca_eagle_lake_cliff.blurb: Eagle Lake Cliff rises above the south shore of Eagle Lake on Tahoe's West Shore, a lovely spot whose cracks rank with the finest around the lake. Most routes are trad, with chimneys and clean cracks, plus a few sport lines, and the grades cluster around 5.10 and 5.11. Space Walk and Seams to Me are among the favorites. The hike in follows Eagle Creek Canyon, and the wall stays in shade through much of the day, which helps on warm afternoons.
ca_eagle_lake_cliff.parking_note: Start from the Eagle Falls trailhead on the West Shore side of Emerald Bay; the cliff is a hike from there.
ca_eagle_lake_cliff.approach: Take the Eagle Falls trail up the canyon, bear right at the junction onto the Eagle Lake trail, and follow the lake's east shore around to its south side, where the cliff rises above the water.

co_quarry_wall_the.blurb: The Quarry Wall is a quiet corner of the North Table Mountain cliffs above Golden, set on columnar basalt. Cracks and jamming dominate the trad climbing, with a good number of boulder problems and a few sport lines, especially toward the right side. Grades span an unusually wide range: easy problems and moderates at one end, and hard sport routes like Kleptocracy and Elephantiasis at the other. It faces the sun and is sheltered, which makes it appealing in cold weather. The rock can be dirty and flaky in spots, and traffic noise from the nearby brewery carries.
co_quarry_wall_the.parking_note: From Golden's main street, take 10th Street east past the brewery complex and wind back around to the gravel lot at the end of Easley Way.
co_quarry_wall_the.approach: Follow the trail west beneath the terraced road cuts to a cairned junction, then double back east above the terraces until you are below the main wall.

co_north_end_the.blurb: The North End is a sector of Shelf Road, the limestone sport-climbing destination north of Canon City. Every route here is bolted, and the grades sit mostly in the 5.10 to 5.12 range, with a smaller group at 5.9 and a few 5.13s. King Coral, The Function and Houses of the Holy are among the better-known lines. Shelf is a popular area, so expect company on good weekends, and note that the limestone is pocketed and sometimes brittle, which is why trad is rare.

co_sundance_buttress.blurb: Sundance Buttress is the westernmost and tallest cliff on Lumpy Ridge, roughly 700 to 1,000 feet of technical granite. Nearly everything is multi-pitch trad, with flared cracks, thin seams and tricky protection, and the grades run from about 5.7 up through the low 5.12s. Kor's Flake, Mainliner and Turnkorner are classic outings. The long approach keeps crowds down, so it feels remote compared with the rest of the ridge. Descent is by a steep gully, and weekdays are quieter than weekends.
co_sundance_buttress.parking_note: Park at the Lumpy Ridge trailhead lot at the end of Lumpy Ridge Road, north of Estes Park off Devil's Gulch Road.

co_third_flatiron.blurb: The Third Flatiron is a huge tilted slab of conglomeratic sandstone on the slopes above Boulder, and its east face is a rite of passage for Front Range climbers. The East Face (Standard) is a long, low-angle route of about eight pitches, with a sparse, slabby crux and fixed bolts to help with route-finding. Harder trad and sport lines cover the other faces, up through the 5.12s. It faces east, so it gets plenty of sun; expect other parties and waits at belays on the popular lines.
co_third_flatiron.parking_note: Start at the Chautauqua Park lot off Baseline Road, then hike up the Royal Arch and Flatiron trails to the base.

_expect.name: Cactus Cliff Far Right (Funkdemental and right)

co_e_cactus_cliff_far_right_funkdemental.blurb: The far right end of Cactus Cliff at Shelf Road is bolted limestone with a strong sunny character, which makes it a good choice on cool days. Nearly all of it is sport, and the grades are concentrated at 5.10 and 5.11, with a few 5.9s and 5.12s. Funkdemental, I Claudius and Affluenza are popular lines. Reach it from the Bank parking area by walking around the corner. Shelf Road is busy on good weekends, and lower-grade limestone here can be slick from polish.
